strengths: Best engine on the panel. Guards, effects and graders are typed expressions that are statically type-checked against the data model (field existence through refs, enum membership), so most logic errors surface at check time with did-you-mean hints instead of at runtime.
Error messages are snapshot-tested as the engine's interface to the model. Each error carries a code, a path, file:line and a hint, which is exactly what 'precise enough for a model to fix' asks for.

Seeding by simulation evolves workflow entities through the real actions on the virtual clock. Seed rows are legal and internally consistent by construction: events exist, timestamps are monotonic, and breaches really happened.

Strongest grader discrimination. Each check must be false at seed, every prefix of the reference must score below 1, an overreach mutant must score 0, a wrong-target mutant must score below 1, and a gate-coverage lint forces collateral checks.

The checker requires scenario coverage per action: a happy path, one failure path per guard with an unchanged state hash, and a timer test. 'Implement logic, then check and test' is therefore verified by the engine, not taken on trust.
The admin surface runs on a separate port the agent cannot reach. Reset uses the SQLite backup API, and a state-hash test confirms reset equals seed.
Per-entity RNG streams keep unchanged entities byte-identical through `update`, so existing tasks keep passing.
weaknesses: The WorldGen agent side is thin. There is no oscillation or stall detection beyond 'same error at same path 3 times', no structured backtracking protocol, no checkpoint/resume, and only about 15 hardening prompts on D9. That is the main risk in the live run.

Graders hardcode IDs (TCK-2207, AGT-0031). This is brittle when the seed is regenerated or changed by `update`, and nothing checks that the instruction gives the agent enough information to find that row.
The task stage has no tool for checking facts against the actual seed. The model can invent facts, and the plan relies on anchors alone.
Simulation-based seeding is complex and slow to build. An LLM-written simulation 'policy' may fail on unusual domains, and there is no fallback to a direct generator.
A custom expression DSL with type-checking is a lot of engine work. Expressiveness gaps on unseen domains push the model to the less-checkable py: escape hatch.
There is little on OpenAPI scale handling (large specs, circular $refs, an operation index) and no conformance diff that checks the world against the source spec.

strengths: Most robust plan for the live run. Repair errors are fingerprinted by (code, path) to detect oscillation, a stall escalates to a stronger model, a patch that adds new errors is reverted automatically, and unrepairable tasks are dropped only while at least 3 remain.

Errors carry an `owner_stage` field. Together with a typed amend(stage, patch, reason) tool and a backtrack budget, this handles failures caused by an upstream stage, and each amendment is logged as an assumption so nothing changes silently.

Deterministic OpenAPI ingest: full $ref resolution with circular-ref cutting, an operation index for large specs, narrowing, a computed schema closure, a log of dropped operations, and a conformance diff of paths, shapes and error codes. CSV ingest profiles in code, finds FKs by value overlap and flags PII.

The plan records the real-world analog (e.g. Zendesk), assumptions, out-of-scope items and open questions with default answers. A code linter checks the plan, and an engine check confirms that every planned item exists in the result.
Logic tests run against an auto-generated fixture seed, so stage 3 is decoupled from stage 4.
A query_seed tool and anchor rows keep tasks tied to real seed facts. Model-written decoys sit on top of code-generated mutants (truncation, collateral damage).

The 30-prompt eval harness includes odd domains, large OpenAPI specs and messy CSVs. The plan also has checkpoint/--resume, saved transcripts, per-role model config, temperature 0, and a seed migration that preserves existing rows byte for byte.
weaknesses: The simpleeval/CEL-like expressions are not statically type-checked against the model, so more errors appear at runtime than in plan A.

Workflow-state seed rows come from state-conditional generators rather than simulation, so their history (event rows, timestamps that line up with state) can be inconsistent. A plausibility linter catches only part of this.
Reference solutions may include clock moves through the admin API, which the agent under test cannot make. The plan does not separate a task's pre-run setup from the agent's own actions.
It does not say whether /_engine admin routes are reachable by the agent being tested.
The collateral cap at 0.5 is weaker discrimination than a hard gate.
It is the most ambitious plan with only about 10 days and no cut lines, so there is a risk of breadth over a solid engine.

strengths: A thin end-to-end slice by Day 2, explicit cut lines, and an engine feature-freeze give the most realistic chance of shipping something that works.
Graders use predicates relative to the seed (seed.*, seed_now) instead of hardcoded IDs, so they survive seed regeneration and `update`.

It has the richest set of code-generated mutants, including running the reference twice to test idempotence (e.g. a double refund) and an over-broad write. A GRADER_TRIVIAL flag catches checks that the seed already satisfies.
The stress suite includes a vague prompt and an impossible prompt that must fail honestly. This tests the 'knows when to stop' requirement directly.

A deliverables checklist maps each spec item to where it lives. The plan also includes concrete Slack questions, a DECISIONS.md, a Hypothesis property test that failed calls leave state unchanged, a determinism double-run, recorded-LLM CI fixtures, and an X-Actor header for workflows that depend on roles.
Seeded 'needle' rows are recorded in needles.json so task writers can target them.
weaknesses: The spec requires all three input types, but OpenAPI/CSV ingest, mutant verification, collateral checks and stage-3 scenario tests are only SHOULD items. Under time pressure they may not ship.
The primary custom-logic mechanism is Python handlers. The checker cannot type-check them and they fail at runtime with vague errors, which hurts self-repair on unseen domains.
The seed comes from a model-written generator.py. That is more code where the model can go wrong, and an AST lint is a weak sandbox.
A collateral failure only caps the score at 0.5, and Python graders are allowed, which weakens the 'graders are declarative and checkable' guarantee.
Only 150 rows minimum per core entity and no seeding by simulation, so realism depends on the generator's quality.
Repair is simpler (one regeneration on no progress), with no ownership routing to upstream stages beyond a model-justified choice.

best_ideas_to_keep: Declarative-first logic: per-entity state machines, actions made of guards and effects, and timers, with a narrow py: ctx escape hatch that runs inside the same transaction and is flagged in the report (A/B).
Statically type-check every expression (guards, effects, grader checks) against the data model, with did-you-mean hints, and snapshot-test the error messages as an API (A).
A stable error catalog. Each error has code, path, file:line, expected/actual, hint, and owner_stage to route repairs (A+B).
State-machine fields marked managed_by/via: action, so a generic PATCH cannot bypass the workflow, for fidelity to the real software (A/C).
One SQLite transaction per request, plus a property test that every failed call leaves the state hash unchanged and does not advance the clock (A/C).

Virtual clock: fixed start, +1s per committed write, reads do not advance it, and jumps only through admin; IDs from per-entity counters; total ordering with an id tiebreak; and a state-hash test that reset equals seed (A).
Admin/inspect API on a separate port or prefix the agent cannot reach. It provides state, diff vs seed, a call log with per-call diffs, reset, clock, grade and hash (A+C).

Required per-action scenario tests (a happy path plus one failure path per guard with an unchanged state hash, plus a timer test), run against a small auto-generated fixture seed so stage 3 does not depend on stage 4 (A+B).

The LLM writes a seed generator spec, not rows. Workflow entities are evolved through real actions on the virtual clock where possible. The result is frozen to seed.lock with a hash and checked by a plausibility linter (every state present, none above 70%, causal timestamps, scenario rows present) (A+B+C).

Grader shape is sum(weight * check) * product(gates). Each check must be false at seed (GRADER_TRIVIAL), and an unchanged_except collateral gate is mandatory unless the task declares an exemption with a reason (A/B/C).

Verify suite in code: reference=1, noop=0, every prefix below 1, an overreach mutant scoring 0, a wrong-target/sibling mutant below 1, the reference run twice below 1 where idempotence matters, a first-page-only mutant, and LLM-written decoys below 1 (A+B+C).
Seed-relative selectors (seed.*, seed_now) and anchor/needle rows instead of hardcoded IDs (C+A).
A query_seed tool in the task stage so instructions rely only on facts that exist in the seed (B).

Deterministic OpenAPI ingest (ref resolution, operation index, narrowing, schema closure, dropped-operations log) plus a conformance diff. Deterministic CSV profiling with FK detection by value overlap (B).

The plan names a real_world_analog and records assumptions with rationale, out_of_scope items, and open_questions with default answers. A code linter checks the plan, and an engine check confirms every planned item exists in the result (B).

Repair loop: patches by default and full rewrite on escalation, (code, path) fingerprints for oscillation, stall leads to a stronger model, automatic revert of regressions, typed amend() backtracking within a budget, and dropping a task only while 3 or more remain (B).
On failure, write to <out>.FAILED/ with FAILURE.md (remaining errors, what was tried, suspected cause, suggested narrower request) and a non-zero exit (A/B/C).
update builds a plan delta, analyzes impact over a dependency graph, re-runs only the affected stages, keeps existing rows byte-identical, and blocks on regressions in existing tasks (A/B).
Checkpoint each stage and support --resume, save transcripts, log events in run.jsonl with tokens, cost and latency per call, and use worldgen.toml for per-role models and budgets (B/C).
A thin end-to-end slice early, cut lines, and a stress/eval suite that includes vague and impossible prompts that must fail honestly (C+B).
gaps_in_all_plans: None of the plans has a solvability check: no plan confirms that a task's instruction plus the API the agent can reach is enough to complete the task. The checker should replay the reference using only agent-facing routes, never admin or clock endpoints, and reject captured IDs that the instruction does not identify and no search path reaches.

None of the plans cleanly separates task setup (pre-run clock advance or state preconditions owned by the harness) from the agent's actions. B lets references move the clock, which a real agent cannot do.

Agent-facing API documentation: none of the plans requires an OpenAPI/tool description for each world so the agent being tested can discover its routes. C lists the export as a bonus and B only gets it implicitly from FastAPI.

Robustness to alternative valid solutions: only A mentions it briefly. Verify should include at least one alternative correct path (e.g. a different but valid search, or a different order of steps) that must also score 1, so graders check outcomes and do not overfit to the reference.

Fidelity linting for description inputs: there is no check against real-software conventions (REST naming, pagination style, status codes, error envelope, required timestamps). B's real_world_analog is only a prompt hint.
Live-run time limits: no plan budgets or parallelizes per-task verify and repair to fit a hard wall-clock limit, or measures p95 build time.
Sandboxing of the Python escape hatch: AST scanning alone is weak. A subprocess with CPU/memory/time limits and no network, run behind the ctx API, is safer.
Concurrent agent calls: the plans use a global lock but do not spell out deterministic ordering under concurrency or how call-log order is defined.
Tasks graded on an answer (e.g. 'how many tickets breached?') are not supported except as an open question in A, so read-heavy tasks cannot be graded.
Realism of seed text beyond distributions: no plan checks diversity or duplication of free-text fields or name collisions, except B's check for duplicate display names among people.
recommended_decisions: Use declarative state machines and actions with a typed expression language, plus a py: escape hatch through ctx that is flagged in the report. Static checkability is what makes self-repair converge on unseen prompts.
Type-check expressions against the model at check time (A), not with simpleeval at runtime (B). Errors found at check time are cheaper to repair than runtime tracebacks.

Seed: the LLM writes a generator spec; workflow entities are evolved through real actions (simulation) and fall back to state-conditional generators plus an invariant sweep if simulation fails. Simulation is legal by construction, and the fallback keeps unusual domains working.

Graders: weighted checks times hard gates (a collateral failure gives 0, not 0.5), each check false at seed, seed-relative selectors plus named anchors. This gives sharp discrimination that survives updates.

Verify = ref=1, noop=0, prefixes<1, overreach=0, wrong-target<1, reference twice<1 where relevant, decoys<1, plus one alternative valid solution=1, with references limited to agent-facing routes. This catches both weak graders and graders that overfit.

The admin API runs on a separate port; task setup (clock advance, preconditions) is declared in the task and run by the harness, never in the reference. The agent must not be able to inspect, reset or time-travel.

Clock: +1s per committed write, reads and failed calls do not advance it, jumps only through admin, and timers fire in chronological order. This makes runs deterministic with strictly ordered timestamps.
Make OpenAPI and CSV ingest MUST items, deterministic and in code, with a conformance diff for OpenAPI. The spec lists all three input types as minimum features.

Repair: JSON patch by default, full rewrite on oscillation, a stronger model on stall, owner_stage routing to an amend() backtrack, and a global USD/time cap. This is the most convergent design without runaway cost.

Run non-interactively by default: open_questions get recorded default answers in plan.md, with an optional --interactive or --pause-after-plan. The live run is likely unattended, and this still meets 'no silent guessing'.
Build a thin end-to-end slice by Day 2, then deepen it, and keep an eval suite of 20-30 prompts including vague and impossible ones. Pass rate on unseen prompts is what decides the trial.
Write failed builds to <out>.FAILED/ with FAILURE.md and a non-zero exit, and never write to the success path. This makes 'knows when to stop' easy to check mechanically.
